title: The storm (Luke 8:22–25)
hook: the boat is swamping, Jesus is asleep, and the disciples shout him awake

segments.voice: Yesterday, a boy's lunch: five loaves, two fish, twelve baskets left over. Your line was it was enough. What did you offer? Today we're back on the lake, and the weather turns. Day fifty-five.

Think of three in the morning, when a worry gets loud. The bill, the diagnosis, the text you shouldn't have sent. Everything feels like it's going under, and everyone else seems to be asleep. Now picture a fishing boat on the Sea of Galilee. Jesus says, let's go over to the other side of the lake, and they push off. The lake sits low among hills, and storms can drop onto it fast. As they sail, Luke says, Jesus falls asleep. Then the wind comes down, the waves come over the side, and the boat starts filling with water. These are fishermen. They know this lake. And they're terrified. Today, the storm.
screen: `3AM, AND EVERYTHING'S GOING UNDER.` → `HE FALLS ASLEEP.` → `THE BOAT FILLS WITH WATER.`

segments.voice: They wake him, in the King James Bible, with a shout: "Master, master, we perish." In Mark's telling they're even more raw: "Master, carest thou not that we perish?" Don't you care? It's one of the most honest prayers in the Bible, and it's shouted at a sleeping man in a sinking boat. And the text doesn't scold them for shouting. Then Luke says: "he arose, and rebuked the wind and the raging of the water: and they ceased, and there was a calm." Mark gives the words he speaks to the sea: "Peace, be still." He talks to the storm the way you'd calm a frightened animal. And then there's a silence so big the disciples are more afraid of the calm than they were of the waves. He turns to them: "Where is your faith?" And they whisper to each other: "What manner of man is this! for he commandeth even the winds and water, and they obey him." In the Hebrew scriptures, the one who stills the sea is God. The psalms say it again and again. So that's the question the story leaves in the boat: who is this? Christians have long seen the church itself as a boat on rough water, and the main hall of many church buildings is still called the nave, from the Latin word for ship. And here's one more thing. Notice that he was in the boat the whole time. Asleep, but there. The story doesn't promise there'll be no storms. It says the storm doesn't have the last word.
screen: `MASTER, CAREST THOU NOT?` · `HE REBUKED THE WIND.` · `WHAT MANNER OF MAN IS THIS?` · `THE NAVE: THE CHURCH AS A BOAT.` · then, large: `PEACE, BE STILL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and feel your feet on the floor. Now name the storm you're in. Not in general. Specifically. The one that keeps you up. Say it out loud, quietly, in one sentence, even if nobody hears. The disciples didn't dress it up. Then take three slow breaths, and on each out-breath let your shoulders drop a little. If you pray, you can shout it honestly, like they did, or say the words Peace, be still. If you don't, just let the breath be the calm. The bell holds the time.
The storm. A swamping boat, a sleeping teacher, a shout of don't you care, and a calm that frightened them more than the waves.
Your line: peace, be still. Today, when the storm gets loud, name it out loud once, and take one slow breath before you answer it. Day fifty-five.

howItsDone: Many Christians turn to this story in times of fear and illness, and it's often read at services for people at sea. The image of the church as a ship shows up in church architecture, in hymns, and in the name nave for the main hall.

fork.reveal: they wake him with a shout. he rebukes the wind and the water, and there's a great calm. the text never scolds them for shouting.

original.note: Greek, from Mark: be silent, be muzzled. The words the KJV renders peace, be still.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice story about a calm lake.
what it means: frightened friends shout at a sleeping teacher, and the storm stops, and the calm raises a bigger question: who is this?
what a scholar hears: in the Hebrew scriptures, stilling the sea is what God does, and Mark's words to the storm, be silent, be muzzled, are the kind used to silence a demon or a beast.

notes: Sudden storms on the Sea of Galilee (low-lying lake, winds off the surrounding hills); commonly described; confirm.
'More afraid of the calm': Luke 8:25 'they being afraid wondered'; Mark 4:41 'they feared exceedingly'. Confirm the phrasing.

'Where is your faith?' (Luke 8:25) is quoted in the voice but its source entry is combined here: KJV Luke 8:25 reads 'Where is your faith? And they being afraid wondered, saying one to another, What manner of man is this! for he commandeth even the winds and water, and they obey him.' Confirm.
Nave from Latin navis (ship); the ship as an image of the church goes back to early Christian writers. Confirm.
Original: Mark 4:39 σιώπα, πεφίμωσο; φιμόω is also used in Mark 1:25 to silence an unclean spirit. Confirm the trapdoor claim.
